extraction_notes: Text PDF (68 pp.); PAGE n below is the PDF page (catalog's printed page number is n-1). Only p.1 (cover) and p.55 (end of a table) are low-text. Catalog is the 2025-26 (FY25-26) Program of Studies; no 2026-27 version was found in Phase 1 (catalog_status outdated_only), so some entries are marked 'Alternating Course: Offered 2026-2027'. Course tables were extracted from the layout text (.txt), descriptions copied by column from there; the .raw.txt is garbled for these tables. Course names/codes/credits/grades come from the table columns; credits are as printed (no derivation needed). Length is only set where the entry says so (year-long / FULL year); otherwise 'unknown'. Courses with Modified/Standard/Honors levels under one heading are one record (level standard, honors_option true); Honors-only courses have level honors; Adaptive PE (Modified only) is special_program. EC (Early College at Your High School, WMCC) courses are level early_college; credits recorded are the high school credits ('1 (HS) and N (College)'). EC Accounting I is printed under both Business and Mathematics; Computer Applications and Personal Finance are printed again in the CTE Pre-Tech section; each kept once. British Literature's printed description is a copy of the Art Illuminates the Dark art description (source error), copied verbatim. CTE programs (BAT, EMS, Fire, Integrated Trades) are run by Canaan itself; recorded as level CTE with provider null; their year plans, certifications and embedded credits are in notes/fulfills_text. Flexible-pathway programs with descriptions (VT Dual Enrollment, Early College at Your High School, Fast Forward, ECP, VLACS, Early College Online, Work-Based Learning, VHS/VtVLC, HSCP) are one record each, notes 'program'. Not extracted as courses: WMCC/CMCC/NMCC approved-course tables (pp.18-20; titles/codes only, no descriptions, many not at CMHS), North Country Career Center programs (named only, p.23), Credit Recovery Program (p.24, a remediation policy), and titles that appear only in the course-selection-by-grade lists (Advanced Math, PE II, Woodworking IV) with no entries in the course offerings. Intro to Technology & Digital Media is called 'Intro to Technology & Social Media' in the selection lists (names in the course table used). Algebra I/II and Geometry have separate Standard and Honors descriptions inside one entry, copied together. Check warnings reviewed and judged false positives: Domination of the Idea, Painting, Algebra I, Pre-Algebra, Conceptual Physics and EC Forestry Resources each continue across a page break, where the table's other columns (name, 'Alternating Course' note, course code/level, prerequisites, 'Fulfills' text) and the running footer print between the two halves of the description; the descriptions were re-compared with the text files and are complete and verbatim (the prerequisite and level text of those rows is recorded in prerequisites/code/notes fields).

courses.description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following historical eras: Prehistoric, Ancient Egyptian, Aegean, Greek, and Roman. The focus will be on how the ideas of ancient peoples have been built upon over time and are still being used by modern and contemporary artists. The course will also cover modern challenges concerning the preservation and viewing of ancient works of art. Lessons in making art will stem from the ideas of ancient artists and their work. Students will have the opportunity to build technical skills and create their own works in the following media: drawing, painting, printmaking, photography, sculpture, ceramics, and other applied arts.
courses.notes: Foundations of Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following historical areas: Early Medieval, Gothic, the Italian Renaissance, Fifteenth Century Art in Northern Europe, Art of Sixteenth Century Europe, Baroque, and Rococo. Even in an era dubbed the “Dark Ages”, people produced amazing works of art. From painting illuminated manuscripts to the construction of light filled cathedrals, the artists of these time periods demonstrated advanced skills and shed light on their subjects during some very adverse and challenging times. Their works of art will serve as the inspiration for students as they develop technical skills and create their own drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, and other applied works of art.
courses.notes: Foundations of Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from native cultures with a focus on understanding how their world view has shaped their art as they have maintained and/or adapted their culture over time. Cultures considered include those of Asia, Africa, Oceania, and the Americas. Ideas and artifacts from these cultures will inspire the work of students as they hone technical skills and create drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, pottery, and other applied works of art.
courses.notes: Foundations of Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following modern historical periods: New Styles in Nineteenth Century Art, Art of Later Nineteenth Century, Art of the Early Twentieth Century, and Modern Art Movements to the Present. Beginning with Picasso, artists rejected traditional views and were driven by new ideas and experimentation. Along with industry and technology, art shaped the fast paced, idea driven world of today in which creativity and invention are highly prized. Students in this class will have the opportunity to be inventive as they develop technical skills in drawing, painting, printmaking, photography, sculpture, ceramics, and other applied arts.
courses.notes: Foundations of Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: The focus of this course will be on the processes used in low-fire pottery. Emphasis will be placed on developing vocabulary, skills, and craftsmanship. Three-dimensional drawing, process documentation, procedural writing, historical research, and art criticism will also be a part of the course. Throughout the course, students will trace the history of pottery from ancient times to the present and discover the science behind this art. Students will be encouraged to embrace new ideas and materials, to think of unique solutions to visual problems, to use the processes to achieve their goals, and to evaluate their finished products.
courses.prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
courses.notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: In this painting course, students will learn techniques associated with watercolor, gouache, ink, and various forms of acrylic paint. If time allows, it could also include explorations of collage, mixed media,and mural painting. It should be understood that drawing is foundational to most other media; therefore, painting preparation will include drawing lessons and exercises dedicated to building the perceptions of edges, space, relationships, lights & shadow, color and gestalt (perception of the whole). Artistic development, and psychobiology of the brain will be discussed in order to understand ourselves and the way we perceive the world around us. We will study the works of the masters and other painters throughout history. The elements of art and the principles of design will be related to both observational and abstract work. Realistic subject matter will include the genres of still life, landscape, and portraiture. As students develop technical skill, there will be an increased emphasis on creativity and pursuit of individual interests through wet media.
courses.prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
courses.notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: In this course, students will create photographic images, focusing on composition, clarity, and contrast. While digital photography will be the primary process used, it may be possible to include black and white film photography and photo editing with Adobe Photoshop. The photographic processes used will be subject to the available equipment, software, and space. Emphasis will be placed on developing vocabulary, skills, and craftsmanship. The course will cover the development of photography from its inception to current times. Process documentation, procedural writing, historical research, and art criticism will all be part of the course. Students will be encouraged to see the world from a photographer’s point of view, to embrace new ideas and materials, to think of unique solutions to visual problems, to use photographic processes to achieve their goals, and to evaluate their finished images.
courses.prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
courses.notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: In this sculpture class, students will create three-dimensional works in a variety of media which may include: plaster, ceramics, wood, soapstone, and found objects. They will explore the four sculptural processes of modeling, casting, carving, and assemblage. If time allows, the class may be able to create an installation. It should be understood that drawing is foundational to most other media; therefore, the course will include drawing lessons and exercises dedicated to building the perceptions of edges, space, relationships, lights & shadow, color and gestalt (perception of the whole). These lessons will increase the students ability to communicate three-dimensional ideas. Artistic development, and psychobiology of the brain will be discussed in order to understand ourselves and the way we perceive the world around us. Students will study the works of the masters and other sculptors throughout history. The elements of art and the principles of design will be related to both observational and abstract work. As the course progresses, there will be an increased emphasis on creativity and pursuit of individual interests in three dimensions.
courses.prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
courses.notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This course is for self-motivated, serious art students who wish to pursue studies in art further than other courses have allowed. College bound students may use this time to accumulate work for a college portfolio. Other students may have a particular media that they want to explore in-depth. Projects and topics of study are proposed by the students, although some assignments may be given. In addition to studio projects, students will submit weekly sketchbooks and writing assignments. Writing topics will include art processes, art history, art criticism, current events, and moral/ethical questions in art. Emphasis is placed on skill, creativity, problem solving, experimentation, self-direction and self-critique. The product of the semester’s work will be an exhibition which communicates a progression of skills and ideas.
courses.prerequisites: Students will have taken a minimum of two art courses. More consideration will be given to students who have taken more than one Foundations and all offered Upper Level courses.
courses.notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Level listed: Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: Students will learn basic double-entry accounting and produce a worksheet, Income Statement, and Balance Sheet. A computer tutorial will enhance the students’ mastery of the subject. This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration and Technology program or a stand-alone course.

courses.description: This course covers operating systems and a range of the most common applications in business and industry. It teaches intermediate to advanced skills in word-processing software, presentation software, and database creation and management, placing special emphasis on spreadsheet and data manipulation. The course also addresses the way these applications integrate with one another. Students explore other business applications and technologies, as well, including collaboration, data storage, and content development. This course is an embedded year-long course within the Business Administration and Technology (BAT) program. This course fulfills the Computer Applications graduation requirement.
courses.provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
courses.fulfills_text: This course fulfills the Computer Applications graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College).

courses.description: This course is designed to familiarize students with word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, and computer technology terms. Students will complete a variety of projects using the G Suite applications and use the Internet in an ethical manner to research, communicate, collaborate, and efficiently retrieve information.
courses.fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Computer Applications is required for graduation
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard). Also listed as a Pre-Tech Foundation Course for Business Administration & Technology (p.59).

courses.description: The main objective of this course is to train students in the use of design techniques in order to create visual presentation environments. The course teaches students basic visual techniques that will enable them to design an attractive environment for the presentation of a product or service, and then actually use the thematic elements to create cohesive and captivating presentations using presentation software, displays, and handouts. The course also helps students develop skills in organization, expressiveness, communication, and creativity. This course is an embedded year-long course within the Business Administration and Technology (BAT) program.

courses.notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.19) maps it to WMCC COMP125W, 3 credits.

courses.description: This course consists of 3 modules: 1) Entrepreneur - This module will give students an overview of themselves to find a better fit in deciding a business career. 2) Overview of Business - This module will focus on how a business is established. The art of work teams will be practiced and used in decision making. 3) Business Career Goals - This module will contribute toward giving the student an ability to choose a business career. The importance of planning will be discussed. This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration & Technology (BAT) program or a stand-alone course.

courses.description: This course will incorporate logic and problem solving with various business applications to deal with ethical issues. Case problems will be systematically analyzed to better understand the concepts involved in making business management decisions. This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration & Technology (BAT) program or a stand-alone course.

courses.description: Students will explore the dynamic world of modern technology through hands-on experiences in podcasting, video production, and digital storytelling. Students will learn the basics of audio and video production, including scripting, recording, editing, and publishing content across digital platforms. They will also gain an understanding of responsible digital citizenship, media literacy, and the impact of technology on communication and society. Projects will include creating original podcasts, filming and editing short videos, and engaging with industry-standard tools and software.
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard). The course-selection lists (pp.28-31) call this 'Intro to Technology & Social Media' and list 'Intro to Technology & Digital Media' as a ninth-grade elective.

courses.description: The focus will be on both marketing theory and practice. The text will introduce consumerism, pricing, motivation, and sales promotion. The student will be responsible for writing a marketing plan for the school store and implementing parts of the plan. This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration & Technology (BAT) program or a stand-alone course.
courses.provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)

courses.description: This course involves students in the process of creating a publication. It integrates graphic design, desktop publishing, digital photography, finance, online activities and public relations. The major production is the yearbook and/or supplement to the yearbook. Due to the nature of the product, students taking the course are expected to be responsible and self-motivated. This is a FULL year course.
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard).

courses.description: This course will explore the richness of American literature as well as the stories that caused them to be written. The course will explore Native American and early colonial writings and then branch out into the giants of the 19th and 20th centuries before ending with modern American classics. There are too many works to list here, but among the titles considered for this course are The Crucible, The Scarlet Letter, various short works and poetry by Poe and others, The Great Gatsby, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, The Grapes of Wrath, The Old Man and the Sea, Our Town, Death of a Salesman, and The Things They Carried. Non-fiction reading will come in the form of articles, research, etc. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 9th grade writing as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Students will be exposed to various types of writing, including informational/ explanatory, argumentative, and narrative. There will be instruction on English mechanics and vocabulary will be geared toward SAT preparation. Frequent homework will be assigned, along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and to participate. The honors course differs from the standard in terms of the amount and depth of reading, vocabulary and writing assignments. Some literature selections will differ between honors and standard.

courses.description: In this course, students will focus on developing creativity through original forms of descriptive writing, poetry, drama and fiction. Vivid vocabulary development, and creative writing techniques will be explored while working on essential worldbuilding skills. Students will have opportunities to take part in writing contests and to submit their work on the Young Writer's Project website. Elements of fiction and poetry writing will include character development, setting, plot, sensory details, imagery, figurative language and sound devices. Among the units considered for this course are Modified Fairy Tales, Gothic Literature, Fantasy, Science Fiction, Media Critique, Realistic, and Adventure. (Course is offered in the Fall.)
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
courses.offering_note: Course is offered in the Fall.
courses.notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the principles of writing and organizing stories for publication in print and electronic mediums, as well as getting students ready for the transition into the career world. Students will develop and compose news stories, learn and adhere to industry-standard style guidelines, conduct meaningful and appropriate research, and understand how the ethics, laws, and culture of journalism influence the media. Students will also create a working resume, cover letter, and work on college admissions essays. (Course is offered in the Spring.)
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
courses.offering_note: Course is offered in the Spring.
courses.notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This course will explore modern literature from the 20th and 21st centuries. There are too many works to list here, but among the titles considered for this course are The Great Gatsby, To Kill a Mockingbird, The Grapes of Wrath, Death of a Salesman, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, The Devil in the White City and In Cold Blood. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 10th grade writing as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Students will be exposed to various types of writing, including informational/explanatory, argumentative, and literary analysis. There will be instruction on English mechanics and vocabulary will be geared toward SAT preparation. Frequent homework will be assigned along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and participate. The honors course differs from the standards in terms of the amount and depth of reading, vocabulary and writing assignments. Also, some literature selections will differ.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
courses.notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This elective upper level course is designed to expand students' literary horizons beyond their English and American heritage to include the study of masterworks of world literature. Students will come to a greater appreciation of and reverence for “foreign” cultural traditions, values, and attitudes, while at the same time identifying those elements which bind all humans together. Students will utilize critical reading and thinking skills, increase their knowledge of vocabulary, develop expository writing skills, produce a research paper, and engage in team learning activities. Students will read a variety of texts, both fiction and nonfiction, from global authors both modern and historical. Reading selections will come from Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, East Asia, and Eastern Europe. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 11th grade writing and reading as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Frequent homework will be assigned, along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and to participate. The honors course differs from the standard in terms of the amount and depth of reading and the amount and length of writing assignments. Some literature selections will differ between honors and standard.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
courses.notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

courses.description: This course deals with physical, emotional, social and mental well-being. It looks at you as a healthy, whole person. The main topics discussed are: family health, mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, personal health habits, consumer health, substance abuse, and birth control information. Expectations of the course include: class participation, personal reflection, fitness days, and public speaking.
courses.fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Health is required for graduation
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard).

courses.description: Standard: This first-year algebra course is designed to help students develop an understanding of variables, linear and quadratic functions, exponents and exponential functions, radicals, factoring, and polynomials. Special emphasis is placed on graphing and problem solving. Not recommended for college bound students. Honors: This is a fast paced first-year Algebra course designed to help students develop an understanding of variables, exponents, radicals factoring, polynomials, and rational expressions. Special emphasis is placed on graphing and problem-solving skills.
courses.prerequisites: Standard: Score of 60+ on the Algebra readiness assessment 232 on NWEA testing; Honors: Score of 70+ on the Algebra readiness assessment, Pre-Algebra 85%, or 238 on NWEA testing
courses.notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

courses.description: Standard: This course is a continuation of Algebra. The concepts of Algebra I are applied and expanded. Additional topics will include in-depth work with quadratics, polynomial functions, their properties, and applications. Trigonometric functions, logarithms, conic sections, sequences and series, rational equations, probability and statistics will be explored. Not recommended for college bound students. Honors: This course is a continuation of Algebra I Honors. The concepts of Algebra I are applied and expanded. Additional topics include working with basic functions, their properties, and applications, trigonometric functions, analytic geometry, systems of equations, polynomials, relations and functions of the first, second, and third degree, real exponents, logarithms, conic sections, sequences and series, probability and statistics.
courses.prerequisites: Standard: Algebra I (Standard or Honors); Honors: Algebra I Honors - a student who takes a full year or two semester to complete Algebra I is not eligible for Algebra II Honors.
courses.notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

courses.description: Topics covered include trigonometry, logarithms, analytic geometry, limits and continuity, differentiation of all types of Algebraic functions, inverse functions, concepts of integration, including basic tools for integrating on both the open and closed interval. Strong emphasis will be placed on the application of these skills. This course will be offered in the spring.
courses.provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
courses.offering_note: Alternating Course: Offered 2026-2027; offered in the spring
courses.notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.18) maps it to WMCC 'Calculus I' MATH215W, 4 credits.

courses.description: Standard: The concepts of two and three-dimensional geometry are integrated throughout the course. A major goal of the course is to help students develop logical methods of thinking. The topics also include coordinate geometry, geometric figures, triangles, surface area, volume, circles and trigonometry. Honors: This course places equal emphasis on geometric theory and application. The concepts of two and three-dimensional geometry are integrated throughout the course. A major goal of the course is to help students develop rigorous and logical, systematic methods of thinking. Therefore, proofs, and constructions are emphasized. The topics also include basic figures, proofs, coordinate geometry, constructions, and trigonometry.
courses.prerequisites: Standard: Algebra I Standard; Honors: Algebra I Honors
courses.notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

courses.description: Life Skills Math should not be taken for credit after a student passes Algebra 1. It is an introductory course for students that need remediation of basic math skills. Life Skills Math provides learners with math skills related to activities of daily living. Students will participate in a simulation of real-life mathematical issues, including earning money through a job, writing checks and paying bills with other forms of payment. Topics explored include identifying numbers as they relate to daily living, basic computations, understanding money value concepts, budgeting, measurement, time management, graphic representation, and elapsed time.
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard).

courses.description: This course will inform students how individual choices directly influence occupational goals and future earnings potential. Real world topics covered will include income, money management, spending and credit, as well as saving and investing. Students will design personal and household budgets utilizing checking and saving accounts, gain knowledge in finance, debt and credit management, and evaluate and understand insurance and taxes. This course will provide a foundational understanding for making informed personal financial decisions leading to financial independence.
courses.fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Personal Finance is required for graduation
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard). Also listed as a Pre-Tech Foundation Course for Business Administration & Technology (p.59).

courses.description: This course is a prerequisite for Algebra 1. Topics covered include operations with fraction, decimals, radicals, linear equations in one and two variables, applications, graphing, elementary geometry, proportions and ratios, including percent problems, and problem-solving skills.
courses.notes: Level 2 (Standard). Grade placement column: 'Typically taken during 9th grade'.

courses.description: This course develops those topics required to prepare a student for a Calculus course. There is a strong emphasis on the algebra of functions, especially as they apply to trigonometry. Topics include geometric concepts, trigonometry, identities, vectors, exponents and logarithms, graphing techniques, analytic geometry, complex numbers, limits and continuity, and sigma notation. Applications and pattern recognition will be emphasized. This course should be offered in the fall.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, Algebra II, Geometry Honors
courses.provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)

courses.description: Quantitative Reasoning is a course for students that do not see themselves going into a math/science related college program. This course covers a variety of topics which will provide a foundation for further courses in mathematics as well as other academic areas. Topics covered include set theory, logic, algebra, linear equalities and inequalities, the metric system, financial math, probability, and an introduction to trigonometry.
